relearning.title: Read: variables and fair tests
relearning.description: A short reading with the fair-race analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

sections.title: Change one thing, measure one thing

body.text:
**I can use lab equipment correctly and use the scientific method.**

**Think of a fair race.** To find out which shoes make you run faster, run the same distance on the same track on the same day, and change only the shoes. If you also switch from grass to pavement, you can't tell what made the difference. An experiment works the same way: change one thing, measure one thing, and keep everything else the same.

**Variables.** The **independent variable (IV)** is what the experimenter changes. The **dependent variable (DV)** is what is measured during the procedure. **Constants** are kept the same to get reliable data. The **control group** is the baseline group you compare the experimental data to. It gets none of the treatment.

**Hypothesis.** A testable prediction written **If... then... because...** The IV goes in the If part, the DV prediction goes in the then part, and the because gives a reason from what you already know. It is not a guess.

**Lab equipment.** Read a graduated cylinder at eye level from the bottom of the **meniscus**. Zero the digital scale **with the weigh boat on it, before** you add chemicals.

**Worked example:** A group waters bean plants with 25 mL, 50 mL or 75 mL a day and measures their height after 2 weeks. Water was changed, so it is the **IV**. Height was measured, so it is the **DV**. Seed type, soil, sunlight and pot size stay the same, so they are **constants**. Hypothesis: If plants get more water each day, then they will grow taller, because plants use water to grow.

checks.prompt: A group tests how the length of a pendulum's string affects the time for one swing. They use strings 20 cm, 40 cm and 60 cm long. What is the dependent variable?
checks.explanation: The group measures the time for one swing, so time is the DV. The string length is what they changed (the IV), and the mass should stay the same (a constant). Mixing up changed and measured is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A group tests whether a new plant food helps tomato plants grow. One set of plants gets the plant food. Another set gets the same soil, water and light, but no plant food. What is the set with no plant food called?
checks.explanation: The control group gets none of the treatment, so it is the baseline you compare to. A constant is a thing you keep the same, like the soil, not a group. Mixing up the control group and constants is the common mistake.

sections.title: Graphs, lab reports and lab tools

body.text:
**Tables and graphs.** The IV is always the first column of a data table, and it goes on the **x-axis**. The DV goes on the **y-axis**. The title is **DV vs. IV**.

**Worked example 2:** A group heats water for 1, 2, 3 and 4 minutes and measures its temperature. They chose the heating time, so it is the IV: first column and x-axis. They measured the temperature, so it is the DV: second column and y-axis. Title: **Temperature vs. Heating Time**.

**The lab report** follows the scientific method: **Problem, Hypothesis, Procedure, Observations, Analysis, Conclusion.** The problem asks "How does [IV] affect [DV]?" Observations hold the data tables. Analysis holds the graphs and calculations.

**Two more words.** A **confounding variable** is an environmental factor beyond your control, like the sun coming out during an outdoor test. **Bias** is an opinion based on beliefs instead of data.

**More on lab equipment.** To measure 5 g of salt: turn on the scale, set the empty weigh boat on it, zero it, then add salt until it reads 5.00 g. Goggles stay on, even through clean up. Fire extinguisher: **PASS** (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep).

**Watch out for:** calling the control group a constant (the control is a baseline group, not a thing you hold the same), putting the IV on the y-axis or writing the title backwards, changing two things at once, reading the top of the meniscus, and adding chemicals before zeroing the scale.

checks.prompt: A group times how long an ice cube takes to melt in rooms set to 15 °C, 20 °C and 25 °C. What is the correct graph title?
checks.explanation: The title is DV vs. IV. Melting time was measured (DV) and room temperature was chosen (IV), so it is Melting Time vs. Room Temperature. Writing the title backwards is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A student sets an empty weigh boat on a digital scale. What should they do next, before adding any salt?

options.text: Zero the scale with the weigh boat on it
Take the boat off and pour the salt right onto the scale
Add the salt first, then zero the scale

checks.explanation: Zero the scale with the weigh boat on it before adding chemicals. Then the reading shows only the salt. Zeroing after the salt is in erases the salt's mass, which is the common mistake.

relearning.title: Do: flip the variables, then plan a test step by step
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a worked problem one step at a time.

cards.back: What the experimenter changes. It goes first in the data table and on the x-axis.
What is measured during the procedure. It goes on the y-axis.
Things kept the same so the data is reliable, like the same soil and pot size.
The baseline group. It gets none of the treatment, and you compare the other groups to it.
A testable prediction written If... then... because... It is not a guess.
DV vs. IV, like Plant Height vs. Water per Day.
The curve on top of a liquid. Read a graduated cylinder at eye level, from the bottom of the curve.

checks.prompt: A group sets a ramp at 10°, 20° and 30° and measures how far a marble rolls. Where does the ramp angle go on the graph?

options.text: It does not go on the graph

checks.explanation: The group changed the ramp angle, so it is the IV, and the IV goes on the x-axis. The distance (the DV) goes on the y-axis. Swapping the axes is the common mistake.

options.text: Do thicker paper towels soak up more water?
If paper towels are thicker, then they will soak up more water, because they have more space to hold water.
Brand X paper towels are the best.

checks.explanation: A hypothesis has all three parts: If (the IV), then (the DV prediction), because (a reason). The first choice is a question, not a prediction, and "the best" is an opinion. Writing a question instead of a prediction is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: In a test of whether music helps plants grow, every plant gets the same soil, the same pot and 50 mL of water a day. What are the soil, the pot and the water?
checks.explanation: Things kept the same for every plant are constants. The control group is a whole group of plants that gets no music. Calling constants the control group is the common mistake.

sections.title: Worked problem: plan a fair test

body.problem: A group tests how water temperature affects how fast an antacid tablet dissolves. They use water at 10 °C, 25 °C, 40 °C and 55 °C and time each tablet with a stopwatch. Plan the experiment.

steps.text: Find the IV. The group chose the water temperatures, so the IV is water temperature (°C).
Find the DV. They time each tablet, so the DV is the time to dissolve (s).
List the constants: the same amount of water, the same kind and size of tablet, and the same cup. Only the temperature changes.

Write the problem and the hypothesis. Problem: How does water temperature affect the time for a tablet to dissolve? Hypothesis: If the water is warmer, then the tablet will dissolve faster, because the particles in warmer water move faster.
Set up the table and graph. First column and x-axis: Water Temperature (°C). Second column and y-axis: Time to Dissolve (s). Title: Time to Dissolve vs. Water Temperature.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a group adds 0, 1, 2 or 3 spoonfuls of salt to the same amount of water and measures the temperature at which it boils. What is the DV?
checks.explanation: The group measures the boiling temperature, so it is the DV. The salt is what they changed (the IV), and the amount of water is a constant. Mixing up changed and measured is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A group adds 0, 1, 2 or 3 spoonfuls of salt to water and measures the boiling temperature. Which graph setup is correct?

options.text: x-axis: Salt (spoonfuls). y-axis: Boiling Temperature (°C). Title: Boiling Temperature vs. Salt
x-axis: Boiling Temperature (°C). y-axis: Salt (spoonfuls). Title: Salt vs. Boiling Temperature
x-axis: Salt (spoonfuls). y-axis: Boiling Temperature (°C). Title: Salt vs. Boiling Temperature

checks.explanation: The IV (salt) goes on the x-axis and the DV (boiling temperature) goes on the y-axis. The title is DV vs. IV: Boiling Temperature vs. Salt. Choice c has the right axes but a backwards title, the most common slip.

checks.prompt: A group wants to know if the type of ball affects how high it bounces. Which plan is a fair test?

options.text: Drop every ball from the same height onto the same floor
Drop each ball from a different height onto the same floor
Drop one ball onto carpet and the other balls onto tile

checks.explanation: Like a fair race, change one thing (the ball) and keep everything else the same (the height and the floor). Changing the height or the floor too means you can't tell what made the difference. Changing two things at once is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: In that test, the group changes the type of ball and measures how high it bounces. What is the type of ball?
checks.explanation: The type of ball is what the group changes, so it is the IV. The bounce height is measured, so it is the DV. Mixing up changed and measured is the common mistake.

sections.title: Nature of Science (Amoeba Sisters)

checks.prompt: A group tests whether a sports drink helps runners recover. One group of runners drinks the sports drink. Another group gets the same run and rest, but drinks only plain water. What is the plain-water group?
checks.explanation: The control group gets none of the treatment (no sports drink), so it is the baseline you compare to. A constant is a thing you keep the same, like the length of the run, not a group. Calling the control group a constant is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A group makes paper airplanes from 1, 2 or 3 sheets of paper and measures how far each one flies. Where does the flight distance go on the graph?

options.text: It does not go on the graph

checks.explanation: The flight distance is measured, so it is the DV, and the DV goes on the y-axis. The number of sheets (the IV) goes on the x-axis. Swapping the axes is the common mistake.
